title: The Vega, the Duende, and the Road Above Víznar
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Fuente Vaqueros, the house on Calle de la Trinidad
stops.date_confidence: attested. Birth date and address per the Centro Federico García Lorca institutional chronology and en.wikipedia. Coordinates are the village of Fuente Vaqueros per en.wikipedia (37.21667, -3.78306); the birth house, now the Casa Museo, stands within the village core at roughly 37.222, -3.782. An earlier pin of 37.2306, -3.8172 circulating in the working material is about 3.6 km out, in open Vega farmland, and has been corrected here.
stops.campa: About midnight, in a house at 4 Calle de la Trinidad in a village of the irrigated Vega west of Granada, Vicenta Lorca Romero, the village schoolmistress, gives birth to a first son by Federico García Rodríguez, a landowner grown prosperous on sugar beet. Around the house the Vega is water and poplars, worked by day laborers on other men's land. The boy is slow to walk and quick to sing, and he will keep the accent of these fields in his mouth for life. Six days after the birth he is carried to the parish church and baptized Federico del Sagrado Corazón de Jesús.
suggested_refs: The Casa Museo Federico García Lorca at 4 Calle de la Trinidad, Fuente Vaqueros
Centro Federico García Lorca institutional chronology, centrofedericogarcialorca.es
sources: Centro Federico García Lorca chronology, centrofedericogarcialorca.es/es/fgl

stops.name: Valderrubio, the second village
stops.date_confidence: year genuinely disputed and not resolved here. es.wikipedia ('Federico García Lorca'; 'Valderrubio') dates the family's move to 1905; the Centro Federico García Lorca chronology says 'entre 1906 y 1907'; en.wikipedia gives 1905/1906-07. Dated 1906-01-01 only to order the segment. The renaming of Asquerosa to Valderrubio on 15 August 1943 is attested (es.wikipedia). Coordinates per es.wikipedia 'Valderrubio' (37.234444, -3.823611), correcting an earlier pin 4.5 km to the south-southeast.
stops.campa: The family moves a few kilometres north to Asquerosa, a village whose name means the disgusting one and which will not be renamed Valderrubio until 1943. Federico attends primary school among the children of farm laborers and servants. He learns the ballads the women sing over the washing and the stories the fieldhands tell at the ditches. He also learns which houses in a village keep their doors shut and their windows shuttered. Thirty years later the last play he finishes is about the shut house of a neighbour here.
suggested_refs: The Casa-Museo de Valderrubio, the family house in the second village
sources: Centro Federico García Lorca chronology, centrofedericogarcialorca.es/es/fgl

stops.name: Almería, the house of Antonio Rodríguez Espinosa
stops.date_confidence: contested and tagged inconsistently in the working material, [A] under geography and [R] under chronology. es.wikipedia has him boarding with Rodríguez Espinosa from 1906, covering the 1907-1908 school year and the following July and August, with illness ending it; other summaries give 1908-1909. Dated 1907-09-01 here as the best-supported school year. The illness is given variously as an abscess or a phlegmon of the mouth. Coordinates are central Almería, about 600 m from the city centre; the exact boarding house is not documented in reachable sources.
stops.campa: He is sent to board with Antonio Rodríguez Espinosa, his mother's old colleague and the schoolmaster who first taught him letters back in Fuente Vaqueros, and begins secondary studies in the port city. An abscess in the mouth turns to fever, the fever will not break, and he is carried home to the Vega before the year is out. The accounts disagree over whether it is an abscess or a phlegmon. He never boards away from his family again, and the schooling starts over in Granada in 1909.
suggested_refs: Universo Lorca, profile of Antonio Rodríguez Espinosa
sources: Universo Lorca, profile of Antonio Rodríguez Espinosa

stops.name: Granada, the piano and the two faculties
stops.date_confidence: attested for the substance, approximate for the date. The family moved to the city of Granada in 1909 (en.wikipedia); the piano lessons with Antonio Segura Mesa run 1911-1916 (en.wikipedia chronology); enrolment in Arts and Law is 1915 and the law degree 1923 (en.wikipedia; Universo Lorca). Dated 1911-01-01 to open the Granada years. Segura Mesa's death in 1916 as the hinge from music to writing is the standard account and is repeated by the Centro Lorca chronology, not a document.
stops.campa: The family takes a house in the city, and the boy who is no scholar is put to the piano. For six years he studies harmony and composition with Antonio Segura Mesa, an old man who once wrote an opera nobody would stage and who tells him that music is the only thing worth doing with a life. In 1915 he enrols in Letters and Law at the university, where Fernando de los Ríos and Martín Domínguez Berrueta take him up. Segura Mesa dies in 1916. Federico stops composing and starts to write instead.
suggested_refs: The Colegio del Sagrado Corazón de Jesús and the Facultad de Letras y Derecho, Granada
The Rinconcillo circle at the Café Alameda, Granada

stops.name: Baeza, Antonio Machado at the lycée
stops.date_confidence: attested for Baeza and Machado, and for Salamanca and Unamuno, per Universo Lorca's account of the 1916-17 study journeys and en.wikipedia's 'travelled through Castile, León and Galicia'. The fuller itinerary given in secondary summaries (Córdoba, Ronda, El Escorial, Ávila, Santiago de Compostela, A Coruña, Lugo, León, Burgos, Segovia) is not confirmed by the fetched pages and is not asserted here. Month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Berrueta takes his students out of the lecture room and across Spain: Castile, León, Galicia, Andalusia, cathedrals and inns and the casinos of provincial towns. At Baeza the party calls on the French master of the local lycée, Antonio Machado, who reads them his poems and Verlaine's. In Salamanca the rector, Miguel de Unamuno, receives them, and Federico, still more musician than writer, plays the piano for the company. He is eighteen and has begun taking notes in prose.
suggested_refs: Universo Lorca, 'Trips 1916', on the Domínguez Berrueta study journeys

stops.name: Granada, Impresiones y paisajes
stops.date_confidence: attested. First book, published April 1918 in Granada, printing paid for by his father, per en.wikipedia's chronology and the Centro Lorca chronology. Day within the month unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: His father pays the printer for the notes the boy took on Berrueta's excursions: Impresiones y paisajes, prose about churches, gardens, orphanages, and the dust of Castilian towns, dedicated to the memory of Antonio Segura Mesa. It sells almost nothing. It is the only book of his that ever appears at his family's expense. The following year he leaves for Madrid, on the understanding, never formally abandoned, that he is still reading for a law degree.
suggested_refs: Impresiones y paisajes (Granada: Paulino Ventura Traveset, 1918)

stops.name: Madrid, the Residencia de Estudiantes
stops.date_confidence: attested. Move to Madrid and entry to the Residencia in 1919, October per the Centro Lorca chronology; en.wikipedia gives the year. Dalí's arrival in 1922 per the same sources.
stops.campa: He takes a room in the Residencia on the Calle del Pinar, the liberal college that means to make Spain modern by lodging its young men together among poplars and a tennis court. Juan Ramón Jiménez comes to read. Pedro Salinas, José Moreno Villa, and Pepín Bello are in the corridors, Luis Buñuel is there already, and in 1922 a thin Catalan called Salvador Dalí arrives. Federico stays nine years. He publishes little and recites constantly, and the house learns his poems by heart before any printer sets them.
suggested_refs: The Residencia de Estudiantes, Calle del Pinar, Madrid
Juan-Eduardo Cirlot's journey file, which records the Orden de Toledo founded by Buñuel in 1923 with Lorca, Alberti and Dalí among its caballeros
sources: working/journeys/juan_eduardo_cirlot.journey.json, stop dated 1968-01-01, on the Orden de Toledo

stops.name: Madrid, Teatro Eslava: four nights of El maleficio de la mariposa
stops.date_confidence: attested. Premiere 22 March 1920 at the Teatro Eslava, withdrawn after four performances, per the bibliography of Cervantes Virtual as cited in the working material and corroborated by en.wikipedia's chronology of the first play.
stops.campa: Gregorio Martínez Sierra stages the young man's first play: El maleficio de la mariposa, in which a cockroach falls in love with a butterfly and dies of it. The audience at the Eslava laughs in the wrong places and then shouts at the stage. The critics treat it as a boy's joke. It is withdrawn after four performances. He goes on writing for the theatre and stops offering it to managers. Federico is twenty-one, and seven years pass before another one risks him.
suggested_refs: El maleficio de la mariposa, Teatro Eslava, Madrid, 22 March 1920
sources: Cervantes Virtual bibliography of Lorca's theatre, as cited in the working dossier

stops.name: Granada, Plaza de los Aljibes: the Concurso de Cante Jondo
stops.date_confidence: attested. 13-14 June 1922, Plaza de los Aljibes inside the Alhambra, organized with Manuel de Falla, per the Centro Lorca chronology and en.wikipedia's note on the Falla collaboration. The quote is from a lecture given eleven years later and is attached here as the fullest statement of what the Concurso was reaching for, not as anything said in 1922.
stops.campa: Inside the walls of the Alhambra, on the square built over the Moorish cisterns, Manuel de Falla and Federico stage a competition for singers of cante jondo, the deep song of Andalusia, which the two of them hold to be older and graver than the flamenco of the cafés. Professionals are barred. It runs two days, and the singing is done by amateurs, in front of an audience of dukes, painters and foreign critics who have come up the hill to hear an art of the very poor.
stops.quote: The angel guides and grants, like St. Raphael: defends and spares, like St. Michael: proclaims and forewarns, like St. Gabriel.
stops.quote_source: Juego y teoría del duende, lecture first delivered in Buenos Aires in 1933, trans. A. S. Kline, poetryintranslation.com
suggested_refs: The Concurso de Cante Jondo, Plaza de los Aljibes, Alhambra, 13-14 June 1922
sources: A. S. Kline trans., 'Theory and Play of the Duende', poetryintranslation.com

stops.name: Cadaqués, the house of the Dalí family
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1925 stay and the reading of Mariana Pineda at Cadaqués, per the working dossier's chronology and en.wikipedia. The account of Dalí refusing him is Dalí's own, given decades later in interviews and memoirs; it is testimony from one side only and is reported here as such. Month is approximate.
stops.campa: He goes home with Dalí to the fishing village on the Cap de Creus and reads Mariana Pineda aloud to the painter's family in the whitewashed rooms above the water. For four years the two are inseparable: Dalí draws him, argues with him about putrefaction and Saint Sebastian, and will design his sets. Federico wants more than the painter gives. The account of the refusal is Dalí's own, given in interviews decades afterward, and there is no second witness to it. Around the house is rock with no soil on it, and the sea, the first landscape of his life that is not Andalusian.
suggested_refs: The Dalí family house at Cadaqués, Cap de Creus

stops.name: Granada, Huerta de San Vicente
stops.date_confidence: attested. Federico García Rodríguez signed the purchase on 27 May 1925 and the family used the house from 1926 (es.wikipedia, 'Huerta de San Vicente'), which also confirms Así que pasen cinco años, Bodas de sangre, Yerma and the Diván del Tamarit as written or advanced there. Coordinates per the same source (37.170475, -3.609328), correcting a pin about 580 m out. Whether La casa de Bernarda Alba was finished here or in Madrid is disputed; see the stop for 19 June 1936.
stops.campa: His father signs for a farmhouse in the huerta below the city in May 1925, and from the next summer the family keeps it: white walls, a garden, a piano in a room off the hall, and the Vega running out flat to the mountains. Federico works here every summer for ten years. Así que pasen cinco años, Bodas de sangre, Yerma, the Diván del Tamarit, and finally the play about the shut house are written or advanced at this table. The Gobierno Civil of Granada is twenty minutes' walk from the door.
suggested_refs: The Huerta de San Vicente, Granada, family summer house from 1926
sources: Working dossier, household and property section

stops.name: Barcelona, Teatro Goya: Mariana Pineda
stops.date_confidence: attested. Premiere 24 June 1927 with Margarita Xirgu and sets by Dalí (en.wikipedia; working dossier's theatre table). Coordinates corrected to the Teatro Goya's actual address, Joaquín Costa 68-72 in the Raval, roughly 41.3819, 2.1666 per ca.wikipedia, about 450 m from the pin previously circulating. The Galeries Dalmau exhibition of his drawings, 25 June to 2 July 1927, is tagged [R] in the working material, resting on en.wikipedia alone.
stops.campa: Margarita Xirgu takes the risk no Madrid manager will take and stages Mariana Pineda, the verse tragedy of the Granada woman garrotted in 1831 for embroidering a liberal flag. Salvador Dalí paints the sets. The house is with them from the first act. The following day, at the Galeries Dalmau a few streets off, Federico hangs his own drawings for the first time in front of people who are not his friends. He is twenty-nine. The drawings stay on the wall until the second of July.
suggested_refs: Mariana Pineda, Teatro Goya, Barcelona, 24 June 1927, sets by Salvador Dalí
The Galeries Dalmau exhibition of Lorca's drawings, June-July 1927

stops.name: Seville, the Ateneo and the tercentenary of Góngora
stops.date_confidence: the homage itself is well documented for December 1927 in Seville; the specific venue, the Ateneo de Sevilla, comes from the working dossier and was not independently re-verified, so the building is [R] while the event is [A]. The exact day is an ordering device. Romancero gitano, published 1928 by the Revista de Occidente, is attested (en.wikipedia).
stops.campa: The Ateneo of Seville brings Rafael Alberti, Dámaso Alonso, Gerardo Diego, Jorge Guillén and Federico together to mark three hundred years since the death of Góngora, the difficult poet the nineteenth century had buried under its own taste. Critics name the group after this week: the Generation of 1927. Seven months later the Revista de Occidente prints his Romancero gitano, ballads of Civil Guards and knife fights and a moon that comes down into a forge, and he is famous on two continents at once.
stops.quote: Green, as I love you, greenly. / Green the wind, and green the branches.
stops.quote_source: 'Romance Sonámbulo', opening lines, trans. A. S. Kline, poetryintranslation.com
suggested_refs: The Góngora tercentenary homage, Seville, December 1927
Romancero gitano (Madrid: Revista de Occidente, 1928)
sources: A. S. Kline trans., 'Romance Sonámbulo', poetryintranslation.com

stops.name: Southampton Docks, the RMS Olympic
stops.date_confidence: attested. Departure from Southampton aboard the RMS Olympic with Fernando de los Ríos, 19 June 1929, per the Centro Lorca chronology and en.wikipedia. The overland route through Paris before embarking rests on the dossier only and is not independently confirmed, so Paris is not given a stop here.
stops.campa: Worn down by the wreck of two attachments and by the noise the Romancero has made around his name, he leaves Spain with Fernando de los Ríos, his old professor from the Granada faculties, crossing France and England to the docks at Southampton. They board the RMS Olympic, sister ship to the Titanic. He has almost no English and will acquire almost none. He is thirty-one and has never been outside Spain. Fernando de los Ríos is going over to lecture; Federico is going because everyone who loves him has agreed that he should be somewhere else for a while. The crossing takes six days.
suggested_refs: The RMS Olympic, Southampton to New York, June 1929
sources: Centro Federico García Lorca chronology, bio-1929-1930

stops.name: New York, Columbia University: Furnald Hall and John Jay Hall
stops.date_confidence: attested for enrolment, the two dormitory rooms, and the fall move. Furnald Hall room 617 and John Jay Hall room 1231 are documented by Columbia's Rare Book and Manuscript Library blog, which returned an access-denied error on direct fetch in this pass; the claim therefore rests on the Centro Lorca chronology's corroboration. Day of arrival is approximate.
stops.campa: He enrols in Columbia's summer session to learn English and is given room 617 in Furnald Hall; in the autumn he moves to room 1231 in John Jay. He does not learn English. He goes to Harlem instead, and to the Cuban bars downtown, and to the Battery at night, and he fills notebooks with a poetry unlike anything he has written before: no ballads, no guitars, no moon, but wire, vomit, dead numbers, and crowds. His name stays on the register through the autumn term.
suggested_refs: Columbia University Rare Book and Manuscript Library, 'Federico García Lorca: Dormlife in 1929'
sources: Centro Federico García Lorca chronology, bio-1929-1930
Columbia RBML blog (cited in the dossier; direct fetch blocked by site access control)

stops.name: Eden Mills, Vermont: the guest of Philip Cummings
stops.date_confidence: attested for August 1929 as the guest of Philip Cummings at Eden Mills, per the Centro Lorca chronology. Coordinates per en.wikipedia 'Eden Mills, Vermont' (44.71333, -72.53000), correcting a pin about 5 km too far north. The subsequent stay at Ángel del Río's Catskills house in late August is likewise attested by the Centro Lorca chronology, though the Bushnellsville coordinates in circulation are wrong by several kilometres and no stop is set there.
stops.campa: Philip Cummings, an American student he met in Granada, takes him north to a hamlet in Vermont: a lake, rain, and a house that smells of wet wood. Federico is unhappy there in a quieter register than in Manhattan. He writes about a child drowned in a well and about his own body as something left out in the weather. He does not stay long. From Vermont he goes on to Ángel del Río's summer house in the Catskills, and from there back down into the city for the autumn term.
suggested_refs: Philip Cummings's Eden Mills house, Vermont, August 1929
Ángel del Río's summer residence, Bushnellsville, Catskill Mountains
sources: Centro Federico García Lorca chronology, bio-1929-1930

stops.name: New York, Wall Street
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was in New York during the October 1929 crash and that it fed the imagery of Poeta en Nueva York (working dossier; general historical record; en.wikipedia). Whether he stood in the financial district on any particular day of the crash is his own later account in lecture form and is not independently documented. Dated to the twenty-fourth as the conventional first day.
stops.campa: He is in New York while the market breaks, and what the city gives him goes into the book nearly undigested: money as a live animal, a crowd that urinates and does not weep, columns of figures with no bodies behind them. He has reached the capital of the twentieth century in time for its first collapse, and he does not read the collapse as a financial event. That he stood in the financial district watching men come out of the buildings is his own telling, from a lecture platform years later. No document places him on that street.
suggested_refs: Poeta en Nueva York, written 1929-1930, published posthumously 1940

stops.name: Havana, Teatro Principal de la Comedia
stops.date_confidence: attested. Invitation from the Institución Hispano-Cubana de Cultura, arrival March 1930, lectures on Spanish lullabies, Góngora's poetic imagery and the architecture of cante jondo, and the friendships with Lydia Cabrera, José Lezama Lima and Nicolás Guillén, all per the Centro Lorca chronology, bio-1929-1930. Day within March is approximate; the train to Tampa and the crossing are attested by the same source.
stops.campa: Invited by the Institución Hispano-Cubana de Cultura, he takes a train south to Tampa and a boat across, and Cuba undoes the New York winter inside a week. At the Principal de la Comedia he lectures on Spanish lullabies, on Góngora's imagery, on the architecture of cante jondo, on his own poems. He meets Lydia Cabrera, Nicolás Guillén, and a very young José Lezama Lima. The island is Andalusia with the misery rearranged, and he says so to anyone who asks. He stays until June.
suggested_refs: The lecture cycle for the Institución Hispano-Cubana de Cultura, Havana, spring 1930
sources: Centro Federico García Lorca chronology, bio-1929-1930

stops.name: Santiago de Cuba, the far end of the circuit
stops.date_confidence: attested that Caibarién, Cienfuegos and Santiago de Cuba were on the lecture circuit sponsored by the Institución Hispano-Cubana de Cultura (Centro Lorca chronology; en.wikipedia). Individual dates for each town are not given by the reachable sources; May is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The circuit runs out beyond Havana: Caibarién on the north coast, Cienfuegos on the south, and finally Santiago at the eastern end of the island. He speaks in provincial halls to audiences who have read the Romancero in reprinted newspaper columns and know some of the ballads by heart. The Institución Hispano-Cubana de Cultura pays and the towns turn out. No reachable record dates a single one of these lectures; what survives is the list of towns and the order he took them in. He talks about the island for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The Cuban lecture tour beyond Havana: Caibarién, Cienfuegos, Santiago de Cuba, 1930
sources: Centro Federico García Lorca chronology, bio-1929-1930

stops.name: Cádiz, the Manuel Arnús comes in
stops.date_confidence: attested. Sailed from Cuba 12 June 1930 aboard the Manuel Arnús, landed at Cádiz 30 June, per the Centro Lorca chronology, bio-1929-1930; en.wikipedia corroborates the year of return without the day.
stops.campa: He sails from Havana on the twelfth of June and comes ashore at Cádiz on the thirtieth, a year and eleven days after Southampton. In his luggage is the manuscript of a book no Spanish house will publish while he is alive. He goes up to Granada, then to Madrid, and picks up the theatre where he left it, older by a continent and by a book he cannot place with a publisher. Ten months later the King leaves the country and the Second Republic is proclaimed. The last six years of Federico's life are lived inside it.
suggested_refs: The Manuel Arnús, Havana to Cádiz, June 1930
sources: Centro Federico García Lorca chronology, bio-1929-1930

stops.name: Madrid, five discs with La Argentinita
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1931, five 78-rpm discs of traditional Spanish songs recorded with Encarnación López Júlvez, La Argentinita, with Lorca at the piano, and for the absence of any known recording of his speaking voice (en.wikipedia; working dossier). Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinates are the corpus's canonical Madrid pin; the recording studio is not identified in reachable sources.
stops.campa: With Encarnación López Júlvez, the dancer they call La Argentinita, he cuts five discs of old Spanish songs, she singing and clapping, he at the piano, the folk material he has been gathering since boyhood pressed into shellac. The records sell. They are still sold. They are also the only recording of him that exists anywhere: his hands, his tempo, his choice of harmony, and not one second of his voice. No recording of him speaking has ever been found in any collection.
suggested_refs: The five 78-rpm discs of Canciones populares antiguas, Lorca and La Argentinita, 1931

stops.name: Madrid, La Barraca takes the road
stops.date_confidence: attested. Appointed director of the university touring theatre La Barraca with Eduardo Ugarte under Ministry of Education backing; en.wikipedia dates the appointment 1931 and the working chronology dates the first tour to July 1932. Both are kept: the company was founded under the new Republic and took the road in the summer of 1932. Exact day of the first performance is not established here. Pinned to Madrid, the company's base; the touring itself has no single coordinate.
stops.campa: The Republic hands him a theatre. With Eduardo Ugarte and the Ministry of Education behind him, Federico builds La Barraca out of university students, has a portable stage made, loads it onto trucks, and carries Calderón, Lope, Tirso, and the entremeses of Miguel de Cervantes into villages that have never seen a play performed. He takes no fee. He works at it for four years, in blue overalls, in village squares, on a stage that comes off the back of a truck.
stops.quote: El teatro es la poesía que se levanta del libro y se hace humana.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Lorca in interview compilations, notably Palabra de Lorca: declaraciones y entrevistas completas, eds. Inglada and Fernández (2017); the original interview text was not reached in this pass and the wording is unverified [R]
suggested_refs: La Barraca, Teatro Universitario, 1932-1936

stops.name: Madrid, Teatro Beatriz: Bodas de sangre
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date, corrected for the venue. Bodas de sangre premiered at the Teatro Beatriz, Calle Claudio Coello 41, Madrid, on 8 March 1933 (en.wikipedia, 'Blood Wedding'). The working material had wrongly placed it at the Teatro Español, reusing that theatre's coordinates from the Yerma premiere; the two venues have been separated here. The Beatriz coordinates are approximate to the Claudio Coello address. The Níjar killing of 1928 as partial source for the plot is [R], from the dossier.
stops.campa: A bride goes off with her cousin on the morning of her wedding and the two men kill each other in the wood. The plot comes in part from a killing at Níjar in 1928 that he read about in the papers, and the play is not a transcript of it. Nobody in it has a name except the bride, the moon, and death dressed as a beggar woman. The Beatriz is full, the notices are good, and for the first time in his life a play of his makes money. Within months a company in Buenos Aires is running it to houses of a size he cannot picture from Madrid.
suggested_refs: Bodas de sangre, Teatro Beatriz, Madrid, 8 March 1933

stops.name: Barcelona, the Conte Grande
stops.date_confidence: attested. Sailed from Barcelona aboard the Conte Grande on 29 September 1933 at the invitation of Lola Membrives and her husband and manager Juan Reforzo, following the Argentine success of Bodas de sangre, per Argentina's Biblioteca Nacional, 'Federico García Lorca: de Granada a Buenos Aires'.
stops.campa: Lola Membrives and her husband Juan Reforzo, who have made Bodas de sangre a hit in Buenos Aires, send for the author. He boards the Conte Grande at Barcelona with a contract to lecture and to supervise productions, and with no clear idea what is waiting. He expects to be away two months. He is thirty-five years old, he is the most famous poet in Spain, and he has never in his life earned the money he spends. His father is still settling his accounts. The Atlantic again, southward this time.
suggested_refs: Biblioteca Nacional de la República Argentina, 'Federico García Lorca: de Granada a Buenos Aires'
sources: Biblioteca Nacional (Argentina), bn.gov.ar, 'Federico García Lorca: de Granada a Buenos Aires'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Hotel Castelar
stops.date_confidence: attested. Arrival 13 October 1933 and residence at the Hotel Castelar, Avenida de Mayo 1152, through most of the stay, per Argentina's Biblioteca Nacional and Universo Lorca's 'Argentinean transcendence 1933'. Coordinates per es.wikipedia, 'Hotel Castelar' (-34.60896, -58.38278), correcting a pin about 200 m out. Note a contradiction inside the corpus: mario_palanti.journey.json, which covers the building itself as the former Hotel Excelsior, dropped the Lorca association as unsourced in the pages consulted for that file. The Biblioteca Nacional page supports it.
stops.campa: He comes ashore on the thirteenth of October into photographers. Buenos Aires has decided in advance that he is a genius and treats him as one for six months: interviews, banquets, radio, crowds at the stage door. In the basement of his hotel the peña Signo meets, and he holds court in it. He lodges at the Castelar on Avenida de Mayo 1152, an Italian pile of a building six years old, and works from a room on an upper floor, which he keeps from October to March.
suggested_refs: Hotel Castelar, Avenida de Mayo 1152, Buenos Aires
The peña Signo, in the Castelar basement

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Teatro Avenida: a hundred and fifty nights
stops.date_confidence: attested for the run of roughly 150 performances of Bodas de sangre at the Teatro Avenida and for the economic independence it gave him (Universo Lorca, 'Argentinean transcendence 1933'). Coordinates per es.wikipedia 'Teatro Avenida' (-34.60944, -58.38389), Avenida de Mayo 1222, correcting a pin about 250 m out. The exact date of the reopening with the author present is not fixed in the reachable sources; late October is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Lola Membrives reopens Bodas de sangre with the author sitting in the house, and the run goes to something near a hundred and fifty performances. La zapatera prodigiosa follows, then Mariana Pineda, then a version of a Lope play he directs himself. The royalties come in weekly, in Argentine pesos, from a theatre eleven thousand kilometres from the Vega. At thirty-five, for the first time, Federico García Lorca has money of his own and does not have to ask his father for any of it. The season runs into March.
suggested_refs: Teatro Avenida, Avenida de Mayo 1222, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Juego y teoría del duende
stops.date_confidence: attested that the lecture 'Juego y teoría del duende' was delivered in Buenos Aires in 1933, and that he shared a two-voice lecture on Rubén Darío with Pablo Neruda there (en.wikipedia; Universo Lorca). The exact venues and dates of both are not established by the reachable sources; November is an ordering device, and the coordinates are the corpus's generic Buenos Aires city pin rather than a specific hall.
stops.campa: In a city that will listen to anything he says, he gives the lecture that becomes his ars poetica. The duende is not the angel, who grants from above, nor the muse, who dictates from outside; it comes up through the soles of the feet, it will not be summoned, and it requires the nearness of death to appear at all. He delivers it here, on the Río de la Plata, and not in Andalusia. In the same season he shares a platform with Pablo Neruda, the two of them speaking in alternating lines about Rubén Darío.
stops.quote: The duende is a force not a labour, a struggle not a thought.
stops.quote_source: Juego y teoría del duende, trans. A. S. Kline (2007), poetryintranslation.com
suggested_refs: Juego y teoría del duende, Buenos Aires, 1933
The two-voice lecture on Rubén Darío with Pablo Neruda, Buenos Aires, 1933
sources: A. S. Kline trans., 'Theory and Play of the Duende', poetryintranslation.com

stops.name: Montevideo, Hotel Carrasco
stops.date_confidence: attested for a Montevideo interlude in January 1934, lodging at the Carrasco, with Enrique Díez-Canedo, Enrique Amorim, José Mora Guarnido and Juana de Ibarbourou (Biblioteca Nacional, Argentina; Universo Lorca). No day-level dates are given by either source. Coordinates per es.wikipedia 'Hotel Casino Carrasco' (-34.8905, -56.0554), correcting a pin about 2 km inland of the actual seafront site.
stops.campa: He crosses the Plata for a few weeks in Uruguay and stays at the Carrasco, the casino hotel standing on the sand at the eastern edge of Montevideo. Enrique Díez-Canedo is there to receive him, and Enrique Amorim, and José Mora Guarnido out of his own Granada youth, and Juana de Ibarbourou. He lectures, he is fêted, he swims. It is the furthest south he will ever stand. He goes back across to Buenos Aires in February with two months of the contract left to run.
suggested_refs: Hotel Casino Carrasco, Rambla de Carrasco, Montevideo

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Conte Biancamano
stops.date_confidence: attested. Departure from Buenos Aires aboard the Conte Biancamano on 27 March 1934 per Argentina's Biblioteca Nacional. The Gardel meeting is [R], tradition only: the working dossier calls it plausible and widely transmitted rather than documented, and carlos_gardel.journey.json carries no sourced meeting with Lorca in its 1933-34 material. Pinned to the corpus's generic Buenos Aires pin; the exact berth is not recorded.
stops.campa: He sails for Spain after five and a half months, seen off by a crowd on the quay. He leaves behind a legend the city has never stopped polishing: that he met Carlos Gardel, that the two of them sang together, that Gardel played him tangos in a room on Avenida de Mayo. Not one document from 1933 or 1934 records it. Both men were in the city, both were famous, and the story was told afterward by people who wished they had been in the room. He is back in Madrid by the middle of April.
suggested_refs: The Conte Biancamano, Buenos Aires to Spain, March 1934

stops.name: Madrid, Llanto por Ignacio Sánchez Mejías
stops.date_confidence: attested that Ignacio Sánchez Mejías died in August 1934 after being gored, and that Lorca's elegy followed (en.wikipedia; working dossier). The goring at Manzanares on 11 August and the death in Madrid on 13 August are the standard record and were not independently refetched in this pass. Pinned to Madrid, where he died and where the elegy was written; the goring itself was at Manzanares.
stops.campa: Ignacio Sánchez Mejías, bullfighter, playwright, patron of the Seville week of 1927, comes out of retirement at forty-three, is gored at Manzanares on the eleventh of August, and dies of gangrene in Madrid two days after. Federico writes the elegy that autumn, in four movements. The first of them keeps coming back to the hour of the wound: a las cinco de la tarde, a las cinco de la tarde, set again after every line until the clock is the only thing left in the poem. It is printed in 1935.
stops.quote: At five in the afternoon. / It was just five in the afternoon.
stops.quote_source: 'Lament for Ignacio Sánchez Mejías', trans. A. S. Kline, poetryintranslation.com
suggested_refs: Llanto por Ignacio Sánchez Mejías (1935)
sources: A. S. Kline trans., 'Lament for Ignacio Sánchez Mejías', poetryintranslation.com

stops.name: Madrid, Teatro Español: Yerma
stops.date_confidence: attested. Premiere 29 December 1934 at the Teatro Español with Margarita Xirgu, amid both success and organized right-wing hostility (en.wikipedia; working dossier theatre table). These are the Teatro Español's own coordinates; they were wrongly duplicated onto the Bodas de sangre stop in the working material and belong here.
stops.campa: Margarita Xirgu, who has been staging him since Mariana Pineda, opens Yerma at the Español: a woman on a farm who cannot conceive, and who strangles her husband at a pilgrimage in the last minute of the play. The house is packed for months. Catholic and right-wing papers call it blasphemous, and organized parties buy seats and come in to shout it down, night after night. From here on the Republic's enemies treat Federico as a political object, whether he is one or not. He is thirty-six.
suggested_refs: Yerma, Teatro Español, Madrid, 29 December 1934, with Margarita Xirgu

stops.name: Barcelona, Doña Rosita la soltera
stops.date_confidence: premiere date 13 December 1935 in Barcelona per the working dossier's theatre table, citing the Cervantes Virtual bibliography; not independently refetched, so [A] per secondary source. The venue was the Teatro Principal Palace and its coordinates were not verified here, so the pin is central Barcelona. The Hotel Majestic banquet and the reunion with Dalí are from the dossier's 1934-1936 section. The Sonetos del amor oscuro, composed 1935-36, were kept out of the censored 1953-54 Aguilar Obras completas and stayed essentially unpublished until 1983-84; the manuscripts have never been located (en.wikipedia).
stops.campa: Xirgu opens Doña Rosita in Barcelona: a woman in Granada who waits for a cousin who never comes back, from 1885 to 1911, while the rose of the title opens red in the morning and is white and shed by night. Catalonia gives him a banquet at the Hotel Majestic, and Dalí comes back into his life for one evening after seven years. In the same year he is writing the sonnets of dark love, eleven of them, which he shows to almost nobody and which stay out of print for half a century.
stops.quote: In Spain they open them. Many Spaniards live indoors till the day they die and are carried into the sun.
stops.quote_source: Juego y teoría del duende, on Spain and its doors, trans. A. S. Kline, poetryintranslation.com
suggested_refs: Doña Rosita la soltera, Barcelona, December 1935
Sonetos del amor oscuro, composed 1935-36, published 1983-84
sources: Working dossier theatre bibliography, citing Cervantes Virtual
A. S. Kline trans., 'Theory and Play of the Duende', poetryintranslation.com

stops.name: Madrid, the interview and the last play
stops.date_confidence: the Bagaría interview in El Sol of 10 June 1936 is attested through the Open University of Catalonia's archive catalogue as cited in the dossier, not independently refetched. La casa de Bernarda Alba was finished on 19 June 1936 (en.wikipedia for the year; the day from the dossier's works table). Where he finished it is contradicted inside the working material: the chronology places him in Madrid, the geography entry for the Huerta de San Vicente claims the play was completed there. The contradiction is left open. The quote is [R]: widely cited to this interview, but the original text was not reached.
stops.campa: He gives Luis Bagaría, the cartoonist, an interview for El Sol. Before anything else, he tells him, he is a man of the world and the brother of everyone, and he will not believe in a frontier a man is asked to die for. Nine days later he finishes La casa de Bernarda Alba: eight women, a locked door, a mother with a stick, eight years of mourning ordered for a house in a village he grew up in, and not one line of poetry anywhere in the language of it. The manuscript is dated the nineteenth of June, 1936.
stops.quote: As I was not worried about being born, I don't worry about dying.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to the interview with Luis Bagaría, 'Diálogos de un caricaturista salvaje', El Sol, Madrid, 10 June 1936; wording per Wikiquote's citation and not verified against the original [R]
suggested_refs: The Bagaría interview, El Sol, 10 June 1936
La casa de Bernarda Alba, manuscript dated 19 June 1936
sources: Working dossier, citing the Universitat Oberta de Catalunya archive catalogue of the interview
Wikiquote citation for the quoted line [R]

stops.name: Madrid, the packet left with José Bergamín
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The episode of leaving the Poeta en Nueva York manuscript at Bergamín's office on 13 July 1936 is the standard reconstruction and was not corroborated by any primary source fetched in this pass. The friends' warnings against travelling to Granada, and his answer about his father's saint's day, come from the memoirs of those friends and are likewise reconstruction, not document. Coordinates are approximate for central Madrid.
stops.campa: Before he goes south he leaves a packet of manuscript at José Bergamín's office: the New York poems, seven years old and still unprinted, for the press Bergamín runs. Bergamín is not in. He leaves the papers with a note and goes to catch the night train to Granada, against the advice of friends who tell him Madrid is safer and that Granada, of every city in Spain, is the worst place on earth for him to be at this moment. He answers that he is going home for his father's saint's day.
suggested_refs: The Poeta en Nueva York manuscript packet left with José Bergamín, July 1936

stops.name: Huerta de San Vicente, the return
stops.date_confidence: arrival at the Huerta in mid-July 1936 is attested (en.wikipedia; dossier). The rebellion reaching Granada on 20 July and the systematic killing of Republican officeholders, unionists and suspected leftists that followed are attested. The Falangist search of the Huerta on 6 August is [R], drawn from the biographical literature, chiefly Gibson, and not independently refetched. The arrest of Manuel Fernández-Montesinos is attested; the date of his execution is contested and is dealt with at the Gobierno Civil stop.
stops.campa: He reaches the Huerta on the fourteenth of July for his father's saint's day. On the eighteenth the garrisons rise. On the twentieth Granada falls to the rebels with little fighting, and the shooting of councillors, union men, schoolteachers, and freemasons begins at once and does not stop for months. His sister's husband, Manuel Fernández-Montesinos, the Socialist mayor of the city, is taken within days. On the sixth of August Falangist squads come through the huerta, search the house, and knock the poet in it about.
suggested_refs: The Huerta de San Vicente, July and August 1936
Ian Gibson, El asesinato de García Lorca
sources: Working dossier, arrest and political violence section [R for the 6 August search]

stops.name: Granada, the Rosales house on Calle de Angulo
stops.date_confidence: attested. He moved to the house of the Rosales family, prominent Falangists, on 9 August 1936, believing their standing would protect him, per Universo Lorca's 'Civil Government (1933-1944)' page. Coordinates are for Calle de Angulo, Granada, and are approximate to the street rather than surveyed to the door.
stops.campa: He telephones Luis Rosales, a young poet he knows, and on the ninth of August moves into the Rosales family house on Calle de Angulo. The Rosales brothers are Falangists, several of them in uniform, and the house is therefore the safest address in Granada. His brother-in-law, the mayor of the city, is in the provincial prison a few streets away, and the shooting of prisoners goes on daily. Federico stays a week in an upstairs room, playing the piano, unable to write.
suggested_refs: The Rosales family house, Calle de Angulo, Granada

stops.name: Granada, the Gobierno Civil on Calle Duquesa
stops.date_confidence: attested. Arrest on 16 August 1936 by a group led by the former CEDA deputy Ramón Ruiz Alonso, and detention in a room of roughly four square metres on the second floor with a table, an armchair, two chairs and a barred window over the Botanical Garden, per Universo Lorca, 'Civil Government (1933-1944)'. The same source dates the shooting of Manuel Fernández-Montesinos in the provincial prison to the same day, 16 August. en.wikipedia's compressed chronology puts both on 19 August; that is a source error rather than a rival reconstruction, and 16 August is stated here.
stops.campa: Ramón Ruiz Alonso, a typographer by trade and lately a CEDA deputy in the Cortes, comes with an armed party, seals the street, and takes him from the Rosales house to the Civil Government building on Calle Duquesa. He is put in a room of about four square metres on the second floor: a table, an armchair, two chairs, a barred window over the Botanical Garden. The same day Fernández-Montesinos is shot in the provincial prison. Luis Rosales goes to the governor, and Manuel de Falla goes, and others go. Nothing comes of any of it.
suggested_refs: The Gobierno Civil of Granada, Calle Duquesa, 1933-1944
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Federico García Lorca' (differing date, recorded as an error)

stops.name: Víznar, La Colonia
stops.date_confidence: [R] for the holding at La Colonia and the transfer; attested for Angelina Cordobilla's visits with food and tobacco on 17 and 18 August and for being told on the morning of the 19th that he was no longer there (Universo Lorca). The names of the three men killed with him, Dióscoro Galindo González, Francisco Galadí Melgar and Joaquín Arcollas Cabezas, are attested. Coordinates per es.wikipedia 'Víznar' (37.23111, -3.55389), correcting a pin about 3.4 km east into the sierra; La Colonia stood in the village.
stops.campa: Angelina Cordobilla, the family's servant, brings him food and tobacco on the seventeenth and again on the eighteenth. She finds him in a brand new suit, writing, refusing to eat. On the morning of the nineteenth she is told he is not there any more. He has been taken up the road to Víznar, to a requisitioned house they call La Colonia where prisoners wait before the last kilometres, and put in a car with a one-legged schoolmaster, Dióscoro Galindo González, and two anarchist banderilleros, Francisco Galadí Melgar and Joaquín Arcollas Cabezas.
suggested_refs: La Colonia, Víznar, holding house for prisoners of the Granada killings

stops.name: Fuente Grande, the spring called Ainadamar
stops.date_confidence: the killing is attested; the date is contested and is not resolved here. Eduardo Molina Fajardo dates it to dawn on the 17th, backed by the Rosales brothers and Ruiz Alonso; Gabriel Pozo cites a letter giving 2 a.m. on the 18th; Ian Gibson argues the 19th on Angelina Cordobilla's testimony, and the 19th is the conventional reconstruction, used here to order the segment. The burial place is unknown. Coordinates per es.wikipedia 'Fuente Grande (Alfacar)' (37.244444, -3.557778), correcting a pin about 4.8 km too far east. The quote is [R]: real and well documented as a boast, with the wording taken from Gibson and not verified against a primary edition here.
stops.campa: They are shot before dawn on the road between Víznar and Alfacar, near the spring the Arabs called Ainadamar, the fountain of tears, which has carried water down into Granada for seven hundred years. He is thirty-eight. The bodies go into the ground somewhere along that road and no man who put them there ever says precisely where. Molina Fajardo dates it the seventeenth, Pozo the eighteenth, Gibson the nineteenth. The disagreement has never been closed and there is nothing left in the ground to close it with.
stops.quote: Acabamos de matar a Federico García Lorca. Yo le metí dos tiros en el culo por maricón.
stops.quote_source: Juan Luis Trescastro, boasting in Granada the morning after the killing, as reported by witnesses to Ian Gibson, El asesinato de García Lorca; canonical wording confirmed across Gibson, Paul Preston's El holocausto español and Francisco Martín Moreno [R]
suggested_refs: The Víznar-Alfacar road and the spring of Ainadamar
Ian Gibson, El asesinato de García Lorca; Eduardo Molina Fajardo, Los últimos días de García Lorca
sources: Ian Gibson, El asesinato de García Lorca, via full-text search corroboration of the Trescastro wording

segments.name: The Grave That Was Never Found

stops.name: New York, Poeta en Nueva York in print
stops.date_confidence: attested for posthumous publication in 1940 in near-simultaneous Mexico and New York editions (en.wikipedia). Day and month within 1940 are an ordering device. The manuscript's later history is corrected against es.wikipedia, 'Poeta en Nueva York': lost for nearly fifty years, resurfacing in 1999 in the hands of Manuela Saavedra y Moreno de Aldama, acquired by the Fundación García Lorca in 2003, exhibited in New York in 2013. The 2013 date attaches to the exhibition, not to the rediscovery.
stops.campa: The packet left with Bergamín reaches print four years after the man who wrote it is dead, in two near-simultaneous editions, one in Mexico City and one in New York with an English version facing the Spanish. Neither of them is printed in Spain. The manuscript itself then vanishes for nearly fifty years. It surfaces in 1999 in private hands, is bought by the family foundation in 2003, and is exhibited in New York in 2013. A new critical edition is made from it.
suggested_refs: Poeta en Nueva York, Mexico (Séneca) and New York (Norton), 1940
The rediscovered manuscript, exhibited New York, 2013

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Teatro Avenida: La casa de Bernarda Alba
stops.date_confidence: attested. World premiere 8 March 1945 at the Teatro Avenida, Avenida de Mayo 1222, Buenos Aires, by the company of Margarita Xirgu (en.wikipedia, 'The House of Bernarda Alba'; es.wikipedia, 'Teatro Avenida'). The working material carried this stop with a positive latitude, plotting it in Iraq; corrected here to -34.6094, -58.3839.
stops.campa: His last play has its world premiere nine years after his death, and not in Spain. Margarita Xirgu, who created Mariana Pineda and Yerma and Doña Rosita and who will not go back while Franco is alive, stages La casa de Bernarda Alba at the Teatro Avenida on Avenida de Mayo, the same house where Bodas de sangre ran a hundred and fifty nights with the author sitting in it. The exiles fill the seats, and so do the Argentines who queued for Bodas de sangre twelve years before, in this same house, on this same avenue.
suggested_refs: La casa de Bernarda Alba, world premiere, Teatro Avenida, Buenos Aires, 8 March 1945

stops.name: Granada, the two-page report
stops.date_confidence: [R] pending direct verification. The 9 July 1965 Granada police report, produced after Marcelle Auclair's inquiries, is cited by the dossier to RTVE's summary of 23 April 2015; rtve.es blocked direct fetch in this pass and the document itself was not read. No lodge register corroborating the Masonry charge has been located. Pinned to the Gobierno Civil, the building where the arrest was recorded. The quoted line is a verified Kline translation; note that the widely circulated variant 'more alive than a dead man anywhere in the world' is attested nowhere but Wikiquote.
stops.campa: Pressed by the French writer Marcelle Auclair, who will not stop asking questions in Spain about how the poet died, the Granada police produce two typed pages: the first admission by Franco's state that Lorca was arrested and shot by rebel forces. The same two pages call him a socialist, a freemason of the Alhambra lodge, and a man given to homosexual practices. The pages are dated the ninth of July, 1965, twenty-nine years after the road above Víznar. No lodge register with his name in it has ever been found.
stops.quote: A dead man in Spain is more alive when dead than anywhere else on earth: his profile cuts like the edge of a barber's razor.
stops.quote_source: Juego y teoría del duende, trans. A. S. Kline, poetryintranslation.com
suggested_refs: The Granada police report of 9 July 1965
Marcelle Auclair, Enfances et mort de García Lorca (1968)
sources: Working dossier citing RTVE, 23 April 2015 [R, rtve.es blocked on direct fetch]
A. S. Kline trans., 'Theory and Play of the Duende', poetryintranslation.com

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Jardín de los Poetas: the bronze head
stops.date_confidence: attested. Bronze bust on a concrete base by Eduardo Carretero (1920-2011), municipal art inventory MOA no. 2477, inaugurated 19 August 1986, the fiftieth anniversary of the killing, plaque crediting the Provincial Delegation of Granada and the Argentine Republic, per the weboeba.com municipal-art inventory record. Circulating claims of a 2014 date or a design by Takutaro Yabushi belong to other objects in the Rosedal. Coordinates are the corpus's canonical Jardín de los Poetas pin, inherited byte-for-byte from carlos_thays.journey.json through jose_marti.journey.json; the corpus holds two other pins for the same garden, -34.575/-58.414 in taras_shevchenko.journey.json and -34.5706/-58.4173 in troiano_troiani.journey.json, and weboeba gives -34.5721/-58.4136 for this bust. The discrepancy is recorded, not resolved.
stops.campa: Fifty years to the day after the road above Víznar, a bronze head of him is unveiled in the rose garden at Palermo, among the poets' busts that Buenos Aires has been collecting since 1914. The sculptor is Eduardo Carretero, out of Granada. The plaque credits the Provincial Delegation of Granada and the Argentine Republic, and the municipal inventory numbers the head 2477. This is the city that gave him the only money he ever earned and the largest audiences he ever had. He was in it once, at thirty-five, for six months.
suggested_refs: The Lorca bust, Jardín de los Poetas, El Rosedal, Parque Tres de Febrero, Palermo; municipal art inventory MOA no. 2477

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Hotel Castelar: the room kept
stops.date_confidence: attested for 2003, when the City of Buenos Aires had his former room refitted as a historical memorial inside the working hotel, per es.wikipedia, 'Hotel Castelar'. Month and day within 2003 are unknown and defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The Castelar is still a working hotel on Avenida de Mayo, and in 2003 the city government has his room refitted as a memorial: the bed, the desk, the photographs, kept behind a door that a guest may ask to have opened. He lived in it from October 1933 to March 1934, six months of a life of thirty-eight years. Downstairs, the basement where the peña Signo used to meet is a bathhouse now. A poet with no grave anywhere on earth has a bedroom kept for him in Buenos Aires.
suggested_refs: The Lorca memorial room, Hotel Castelar, Avenida de Mayo 1152, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Fuente Grande and the Barranco de Víznar, the digging
stops.date_confidence: attested. University of Granada excavation October-December 2009 in the Parque Federico García Lorca by Fuente Grande, costing about 70,000 euros, finding bedrock at 40 cm and no confirmed remains; a 2014 dig under Miguel Caballero Pérez less than half a kilometre away, also inconclusive; a 2016 well theory unsubstantiated (en.wikipedia). For the ravine at Víznar, es.wikipedia states 166 bodies recovered and seven civilian victims identified as of 2025, correcting the figure of roughly 132 that was in circulation. Coordinates are the Fuente Grande ground; the ravine excavations lie nearby to the west of Alfacar.
stops.campa: The University of Granada digs the ground beside the spring in the autumn of 2009, at a cost of some seventy thousand euros, and strikes bedrock forty centimetres down: no bones, no cloth, no shell casings. Miguel Caballero Pérez digs half a kilometre off in 2014 and finds the same nothing, and a theory in 2016 that the body lies in a well comes to nothing as well. In the ravine at Víznar the excavations go on: one hundred and sixty-six bodies lifted out by 2025, seven of them given back their names. None of them is his.
stops.quote: I want to sleep the sleep of the apples, / I want to get far away from the busyness of the cemeteries.
stops.quote_source: 'Gacela of the Dark Death', trans. Robert Bly, Selected Poems: Lorca and Jiménez (Beacon Press, 1973), via poets.org
suggested_refs: The 2009, 2014 and 2016 searches at Alfacar
The Barranco de Víznar mass graves, excavated into the 2020s
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Víznar' (166 bodies, seven identified, as of 2025)
Robert Bly trans., 'Gacela of the Dark Death', poets.org
